paragraphs.source_en: At last Nose opened her mouth: “I have come to ask you about a small matter.” The master received this coldly: “Indeed?” Feeling that this would never do, Nose hurried on: “You probably know me already. I live quite near here, yes, in that mansion on the opposite corner...” “Do you mean the house with the large Western-style building and the storehouse? Ah, that explains why there is a nameplate saying Kaneda there.” The master had at last identified Kaneda’s Western-style house and storehouse, but his degree of respect for Mrs. Kaneda remained exactly what it had been before. Nose began again: “Strictly speaking, my husband meant to come himself and consult with you directly, but he is so terribly busy at the companies...” Her look plainly suggested, “Surely this will work.” The master, however, was not moved in the least. As language from a woman he was meeting for the first time, Nose’s tone from the beginning had struck the master as far too overbearing, and he already felt deeply displeased. Nose said, “It is not as though my husband has only one company; he is connected with two or three besides. And he is a director in every one of them. I imagine you must have known that already.” The expression on Nose’s face clearly said, “Surely now you will be properly impressed.” Now, the master of this house is a man who becomes exceedingly deferential at the mention of doctors or university professors. Strangely, however, his respect for businessmen is extremely slight. He believes a middle-school teacher is far more admirable than a businessman. Even if he did not believe so, his rigid disposition would never allow him to expect favors from businessmen or men of great wealth. No matter how influential or wealthy someone may be, to a man who has resolved that he will never rely on such people, their interests are utterly irrelevant. For that reason, apart from scholarly circles, the master knows next to nothing about other spheres, and in the business world especially he has no idea who is where or what anyone is doing. Even if he did know, no feeling of respect would arise in him at all. For Nose, it had never even occurred to her in dreams that, in some corner under heaven, such an eccentric could be living beneath the light of the sun. She had dealt with many people in her life, and whenever she said, “I am Kaneda’s wife,” there had never been a case where their treatment of her did not instantly change. Whatever gathering she attended, and before whatever person of exalted rank, the four words “Mrs. Kaneda” carried weight and passed with authority; how much more so, then, before such a musty, impoverished old pedant. She had expected that merely saying she lived in the mansion on the opposite lane’s corner would astonish him before she even displayed the placard of her husband’s occupation.

paragraphs.source_zh: 最后鼻子开口道：“我到府上来是有点事儿想要向您打听。”主人冷淡地应付说：“是吗？”鼻子觉得这样下去有些不妙，于是赶忙说：“你大概也会知道，我就是离你这儿不远的，对啦，就是对面拐角那座公馆里的……”“就是那座大洋房带有仓房的宅子吗？哦，怪不得那地方钉有金田的牌子哪。”主人好不容易知道了金田的洋房和仓房，可对于金田夫人尊敬程度还和以前一样。鼻子又开口道：“按理说，本来俺丈夫打算自己来，直接和你商量点事儿，不过公司里太忙……”她的眼神表现出“这回总可以管用了吧”的意思。可是，主人丝毫不为所动。作为初次会面的女人，刚才鼻子话中所用的这种口吻未免过于自大，主人深感不满。鼻子说：“丈夫的公司不仅有一家，另外还有两三家呢。而且都在这些公司里担任着总经理。我想这点你也是早已了解的吧。”鼻子脸上的表情分明在说：“这回你总该老实点啦。”说起来，我家的这位主人，一提到什么博士啦教授啦，他都是非常敬畏的。可奇怪的是，他对于实业家的敬意却极少。他相信中学老师要比实业家了不起得多。即便他不这样相信，他那古板的性格也决不会指望接受什么实业家或大财主的恩惠。不管是什么样有权势、有财产的人，对于一个已决心不再指望蒙受他们照顾的人说来，完全是与己无关痛痒的。正因为如此，主人除了学者的圈子以外，对其他方面的事儿都是一无所知，尤其是对于实业界，谁在哪里，谁在干什么，他都一概不知。即便知道，也不会有丝毫敬意。对于鼻子来说，在天下之一隅，居然会有如此怪人也生活在阳光之下，是做梦也没有料到的。她过去接触过很多人，只要自己一说“我是金田的妻子”，没有人不立刻改容相待的。不管参加什么会，也不管在什么样高贵身份的人面前，“金田夫人”这四个字，行得通，叫得响，现在更何况在一个抱残守缺的穷儒面前呢。她本以为只要一说出我就是住在对面胡同拐角上那座宅子里的，即便不亮出职业这块牌子，对方也会大吃一惊的。
